prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- A well-known Iranian filmmaker has written an open letter calling for the release of journalist Roxana Saberi. In a letter, Iranian filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi blames himself for urging Roxana Saberi to stay in Iran. Bahman Ghobadi said he kept quiet about the arrest and conviction of the Iranian-American journalist at the request of her family. After Saberi was convicted last weekend and sentenced to an eight-year prison sentence, he said he felt he had to do something. He told CNN that Saberi, whom he described as his fiancee, is caught in a "game of politics." In his letter, which has been posted by the International Campaign for Human Rights in Iran, Ghobadi blames himself for urging Saberi to stay in Iran despite her desire to leave. Also, he writes, "My letter is a desperate call to all statesmen ... and to all those who can do something to help." "From the other side of the ocean, the Americans have protested against her imprisonment, because she is an American citizen," he writes. "But I say no, she is Iranian, and she loves Iran. I beg you, let her go! I beg you not to throw her in the midst of your political games! She is too weak and too pure to take part in your games. Let me be present at her trial, sit next to her wise father and gentle mother, and testify she is without guilt or reproach." The 40-year-old filmmaker said that Saberi was planning to leave the country, but he kept her from leaving until his latest film -- which will be shown at this year's Cannes film festival -- was completed. Ghobadi won the 2000 Golden Camera award at the Cannes festival for his feature film, "A Time for Drunken Horses." Saberi, 31, was sentenced Saturday to eight years in prison after a one-day trial that was closed to the public. The decision prompted sharp denunciations from President Barack Obama, as well as other U.S. and international officials. Iranian officials initially said Saberi was held for buying a bottle of wine. The Foreign Ministry later said she was detained for reporting without proper accreditation. On April 9, word emerged that Saberi had been charged with espionage. Saberi's lawyer has said he will appeal the verdict. Judiciary Chief Ayatollah Hashemi Shahroudi has ordered the head of Tehran's Justice Department to make sure the appeals process is quick and fair. Ghobadi wrote that he is "optimistic about her release, and I firmly hope the verdict will be canceled in the next stage of the trial." "My Iranian girl with Japanese eyes and an American ID, is in jail. Shame on me! Shame on us!" CNN's Igor Krotov and Shirzad Bozorghmehr contributed to this report.

**TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) —** Prominent Iranian director Bahman Ghobadi has issued a public appeal for imprisoned journalist Roxana Saberi to be freed, saying he feels responsible for persuading her not to leave Iran.

Ghobadi said Saberi’s family had asked him not to speak publicly about the Iranian-American journalist’s detention and prosecution. However, after she was found guilty last weekend and given an eight-year prison term, he decided he could no longer remain silent.

Speaking to CNN, Ghobadi identified Saberi as his fiancée and said she had become trapped in a political struggle. In an open letter published by the International Campaign for Human Rights in Iran, he expressed regret for encouraging her to remain in the country even though she had wanted to depart.

He described the message as an urgent plea to political leaders and anyone else in a position to assist her. Ghobadi noted that U.S. officials had objected to Saberi’s imprisonment because she holds American citizenship, but emphasized that she is also Iranian and deeply devoted to Iran. He begged authorities to release her and keep her out of political maneuvering, portraying her as too vulnerable and innocent to be involved in such conflicts. He also requested permission to attend her court proceedings alongside her father and mother and to testify that she had done nothing wrong.

The 40-year-old filmmaker said Saberi, 31, had intended to leave Iran, but he convinced her to stay until he completed his newest movie, which is scheduled to screen at this year’s Cannes Film Festival.

Ghobadi previously received Cannes’ Golden Camera prize in 2000 for his feature film *A Time for Drunken Horses*.

Following a single-day trial held behind closed doors, Saberi was sentenced Saturday to eight years in prison. The ruling drew strong criticism from President Barack Obama and other officials in the United States and abroad.

Iranian authorities first said Saberi had been detained after purchasing a bottle of wine. The country’s Foreign Ministry later stated that she was being held for working as a reporter without valid credentials. News surfaced on April 9 that she had been accused of spying.

Saberi’s attorney has said the conviction will be appealed. Judiciary Chief Ayatollah Hashemi Shahroudi instructed the head of Tehran’s Justice Department to ensure that the appeal is handled both promptly and fairly.

Ghobadi said he remained hopeful that Saberi would be released and that the judgment would be overturned during the next phase of the legal process. Referring to her mixed identity, he lamented that an Iranian woman with Japanese eyes and American identification was behind bars, adding that both he and others should feel ashamed.

CNN’s Igor Krotov and Shirzad Bozorghmehr contributed to the report.

The case later escalated, with prosecutors accusing her of gathering classified information and passing it to the United States.

A Tehran court convicted Saberi of espionage following a closed-door trial and sentenced her to eight years in prison. Her lawyer and family denied the charge and said they would appeal.

Saberi had reported from Iran for international news organizations, including National Public Radio and the BBC, before Iranian authorities revoked her press credentials. She remained in the country while working on a book about Iranian society.

In his letter, Ghobadi said Saberi’s continued presence in Iran had been linked to their plans together, including a film project. He urged officials to look beyond the accusations against her and consider her personal connection to the country.

“I, Bahman Ghobadi, Iranian filmmaker, with all my being, request the government and judicial officials to release Roxana Saberi,” he wrote.

Saberi’s detention and conviction drew concern from press-freedom organizations and Western governments. U.S. officials said the espionage accusation was baseless and called on Iran to release her.

# Jailed American journalist’s case draws international pressure as Cannes spotlights Iran

**TEHRAN, Iran (CNN)** — International pressure mounted on Iran to grant imprisoned Iranian-American journalist Roxana Saberi a fair appeal after she was sentenced to eight years in prison on espionage charges, a verdict condemned by President Barack Obama and other Western officials.

Saberi, a 32-year-old freelance journalist who had reported from Iran for several international news organizations, was arrested in Tehran in late January 2009. She was later tried behind closed doors and convicted of spying for the United States — an allegation that her family, the U.S. government and press-freedom groups strongly rejected.

Obama said he was “deeply disappointed” by the sentence and expressed confidence that Saberi was not a spy. His administration called on Iranian authorities to release her and ensure that any appeal was conducted transparently and in accordance with Iranian law.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton also raised concerns about the case, while the European Union and human-rights organizations urged Tehran to provide Saberi with due process. Her attorneys appealed the verdict, and Iranian officials indicated that the case would be reviewed.

The circumstances surrounding Saberi’s detention were clouded by a series of changing official explanations.

Her family initially said she told them she had been detained after buying a bottle of wine, an act prohibited under Iran’s Islamic laws. Iranian authorities later said she had continued working as a journalist after her government-issued press credentials expired in 2006. The case then escalated sharply when prosecutors accused her of espionage.

Critics said the shifting accounts raised questions about the prosecution and the evidence presented at Saberi’s closed trial. Iranian officials insisted the case was handled through the country’s judiciary and rejected suggestions that her American citizenship was the reason for her prosecution.

Saberi, who was born in the United States to an Iranian father and a Japanese mother, had lived in Iran for several years. Because Iran does not recognize dual nationality, authorities treated her solely as an Iranian citizen and did not permit U.S. consular access. Washington and Tehran do not have formal diplomatic relations.

The case also drew attention at the Cannes Film Festival through acclaimed Iranian filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi, whose film **“No One Knows About Persian Cats”** was selected to open Cannes’ Un Certain Regard program.

The film, made largely without official permission, follows young underground musicians navigating Iran’s restrictions on artistic expression. Ghobadi publicly appealed for Saberi’s release and described her as a close companion and collaborator connected to the project. His statement brought Saberi’s imprisonment into the international spotlight just as filmmakers, actors and journalists gathered in Cannes.

Saberi had worked with Ghobadi on the film and was widely reported to have helped with its screenplay. Ghobadi said her detention had left him deeply distressed and called on Iranian authorities to treat her fairly.

Saberi’s father, Reza Saberi, traveled to Tehran with her mother to seek their daughter’s release. The family said she began a hunger strike to protest her imprisonment, though Iranian judicial officials disputed or played down reports about the protest. Her parents expressed concern about her health while maintaining that she had never engaged in espionage.

She was being held at Tehran’s Evin prison, where political prisoners, journalists and dissidents have frequently been detained.

Press-freedom advocates said Saberi’s conviction was part of a broader pattern of pressure on journalists in Iran. They argued that reporting without a valid press card, even if proven, should not have resulted in an espionage prosecution or an eight-year prison sentence.

Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad asked Tehran’s prosecutor to ensure that Saberi and another detained journalist received full legal rights during their appeals. His intervention did not overturn the judgment but was seen as a sign that the case had become politically sensitive amid intense international criticism.

Supporters said the appeal should include access to the evidence against Saberi, adequate time for her lawyers to prepare and an open assessment of how the accusations evolved from an alleged alcohol violation to unauthorized reporting and, finally, spying.

The case emerged as the Obama administration was signaling a willingness to pursue dialogue with Iran after decades of hostility. U.S. officials said they did not want Saberi’s detention to derail diplomatic efforts, but stressed that her imprisonment was unjustified and demanded a fair and prompt resolution.

For Saberi’s family and supporters, the immediate focus remained the appeal.

“She is not a spy,” Obama said, adding that the United States wanted to see her treated properly and released.
